I just want to take a minute to say thank you for all of the kind comments and messages about Milk. It means a lot to know that so many people care about my little old snake are wishing him well. 🤍

If you missed our last post Milk is an elderly king snake. He’s been with me for over 20 years and in his old age developed some health issues which has led to needing a tail amputation. He is recovering well, but needed a little help after not being able to shed completely while his sutures are in. 

In most cases when a reptile has some trouble shedding it helps to soak them in some warm water to loosen up the dried skin. While this did help Milk, I didn’t want to attempt removing any more of the skin around the sutures as it looked like some of his amputation site hasn’t fully healed yet and I don’t want to damage any of the progress he’s made closing it.

items.caption:
Blink is one of the few foxes I have that doesn’t like to be touched so I had never considered teaching him this trick before. 
Yesterday, I was trying to coax him to let me pet him and he kept batting my hand away. This was the perfect behavior for me to try and teach him the trick “shake”. He caught on almost immediately. 

He had the trick nailed down within less than 10 minutes!

Usually when I teach an animal to shake I repeatedly grab their paw until it clicks and they will start to reach for my hand on their own. This is the first time I’ve ever taught this trick to an animal I can’t touch, so I’m very excited and very proud of Blink. 

I absolutely love trick training because it is enriching for them as it requires them to really take time to think about what I’m asking. In the wild they would be using their minds to find food, create shelter, raise young, and survive. They don’t have to think about any of that in captivity, so giving them complex tasks helps to keep them sharp and builds trust as we bond and communicate with each other.

items.caption:
In the spring red foxes drop their thick winter coats to make way for a shorter and less dense summer coat. All of the foxes at our sanctuary are ranched foxes or were bred on a “fur farm” which means they were bred to have unnaturally dense coats, far more dense than a wild fox. This was intentionally bred into their generics so that they would have an extremely plush pelt once they were eventually “harvested”. 💔

This dense coat is far harder to shed than the natural winter coat of a wild red fox. While some of our foxes can shed their entire coat on their own. There are a few that need some assistance. Juniper is one of those foxes. She is very particular in the way she likes to be groomed and usually won’t allow us to brush her. I’ve found the only way to reliably get some of these winter tufts off is to make it a game, which allows me to get a little off each time I touch her.

This process doesn’t hurt her at all and despite all of her fussing she does feel much better once I’m finished.

items.caption:
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and kindness so many of you have shown after Reagan’s passing. The messages, comments, stories, and memories have meant more to me than I can say. Thank you for loving my sweet boy and for surrounding our family with so much support during such a heartbreaking time. ❤️‍🩹

So many of you have followed Reagan’s life over the years that I realized one post could never tell the whole story. His life was full of moments — big and small — that brought joy not just to us, but to so many people who watched him grow up.

So I’m going to share a short series called “A Good Dog’s Life — The Story of Reagan.” Each chapter will highlight a different part of his life and the joy he brought to ours and to so many of you.

This first chapter is The Puppy.

Before the dancing videos…
Before the weather watches…
Before the TV appearances with Little Buddy and all the adventures…

There was just a tiny puppy with a big personality who loved treats, training, food, and most of all — his people.

Looking back at these little puppy moments reminds me that the joy Reagan gave us didn’t start when the world discovered him. It started the day he came into our lives.

Thank you again for walking this journey with us and for loving Reagan right along with our family.

A Good Dog’s Life continues. 🐾

If you’ve been here for a while, I’d love to know…
Do you remember when you first discovered Reagan?

items.caption: We posted this for last years Christmas appeal so the stats aren’t correct for this year. But the message is and I also wanted to include Darren in our messaging, because so much of what we’ve achieved over the years was all thanks to him. ♥️ we are so close to getting to the half way point. 🥺♥️🙏🏻🙏🏻🙏🏻 if we can get to our goal, each rescue will receive $18,000. That is HUGE. Some of them are working on donation to donation just to save dogs as they go. Most of them are turning away dogs because they simply can’t keep up. These dogs do not go on to live happy lives.. they die. I think sometimes the message can be lost in counting the number going up and up but we need to remember WHY we’re doing what we’re doing. It’s to save dogs lives. $18000 saves SO MANY DOGS. So so many. That would have otherwise been left for dead. It’s unfathomable how much impact your donations have because to you it’s just $5 or $50 but it honestly does SO MUCH 🙏🏻♥️ so please donate if you can please do it for the dogs that can’t help themselves ♥️

items.caption:
Listening to Maru, beyond words.
まるは人間のことばを話さないけれど、
今日の気分や、眠たさや、
ごはんのうれしさ、不思議に思うこと、
寄り添ってくれること、
そんなすべてを、静かに伝えてきました。

それは耳で聞こえる「声」や「音」そのものではなくて、
目に映るしぐさや表情、しっぽの動き、
それにただそこにある気配だったり。

言葉にならないまるの声を、心で聴いて、感じてみてください。
すべての声が言葉や音になるとは限らない。感じるための声もある。
「感じようとすること」
そのものがやさしく、尊い。
